claims.text: As-received Q235 steel has a native, thin iron oxide scale.
Salt-corrosion protection in as-received Q235 is controlled by the composition, adherence, and morphology of its native iron oxide scale.
An adherent oxide layer limits corrosion by impeding contact between the electrolyte and corrosion-susceptible material.
At 500–600 °C, oxide formation on Q235 is kinetically slow but the resulting scale remains stable and adherent.
A transition in Q235 oxide stability occurs at approximately 700 °C under deposited Na2SO4–NaCl.
At 700–900 °C, increased ion mobility and diffusion rates contribute to destabilization of the Q235 oxide scale.
At 700–900 °C, a deposited Na2SO4–NaCl mixture fluxes the Q235 iron oxide scale.
Salt fluxing and elevated-temperature chemical interactions cause dissolution, spallation, or phase transformation of the Q235 oxide scale.
Dissolution or spallation of the oxide exposes fresh Q235 metal and thereby accelerates corrosion.
Below approximately 700 °C, salt-exposed Q235 will retain a stable, adherent oxide scale and exhibit minimal mass loss.
At 700–900 °C, salt-exposed Q235 will exhibit oxide-scale disruption and increased mass loss relative to its lower-temperature or non-salt baseline.
Annealing can promote formation of an oxide layer that improves corrosion resistance relative to an unannealed coating or bare 316L stainless steel.
316L stainless steel is a more corrosion-resistant reference than Q235 under the proposed Na2SO4–NaCl temperature exposures.
Coatings or alloying modifications may alter initial oxide formation and make the proposed native-oxide mechanism inapplicable.
A lack of oxide disruption and corresponding mass-loss increase across the proposed 700 °C transition would falsify the elevated-temperature fluxing hypothesis.
